title: Behar: wronging with words (Leviticus 25:17)
hook: the rabbis read "ye shall not wrong one another" as a ban on hurtful words (Bava Metzia 58b)
tomorrow: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Behar: strangers and settlers with God, and your line, we are guests here. Did a shared space get a guest's care? Day four hundred twenty-three.

A man walks into a pottery shop. He has no plan to buy anything. He picks up a bowl, turns it over, and asks the owner, how much for this one? The owner's face lights up. She names a price, starts wrapping it, mentions she made the glaze herself. He shrugs, puts it down, and leaves. Nothing was stolen. Not a coin changed hands. And yet the Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code, lists exactly this moment as a wrong. Today: how a sentence can cheat someone.
screen: `HOW MUCH FOR THIS ONE?` → `NOTHING WAS STOLEN.` → `STILL, A WRONG.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-five says it twice. Verse fourteen, about buying and selling: don't wrong one another. Then verse seventeen, again: "And ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God; for I am the LORD your God." The rabbis noticed the repeat. Money was already covered. So, the Talmud says in Bava Metzia fifty-eight b, the second verse must be about words. They called it ona'at devarim, wronging with words. Ona'ah is the word for cheating someone on a price; devarim means words. The Mishnah gives examples, and they are startlingly specific. Don't ask the price of something you have no intention of buying: you're raising hope you'll dash. If someone has turned their life around, don't say, remember what you used to do. If someone is suffering, don't lecture them that they must have earned it, the way Job's friends did. Then the Talmud goes further. Embarrassing someone in public, it says, is like shedding blood: you can watch the color drain out of their face. The Talmud argues that wronging with words is worse than wronging with money, and one of its reasons is simple. Money can be paid back. A word, once it lands, can't be collected. And notice what the verse attaches to it: fear thy God. The rabbis read that as a warning about the wrongs no one else can measure. Only the speaker really knows whether that remark was a joke or a knife.
screen: `SAID TWICE: MONEY, THEN WORDS.` · `ONA'AT DEVARIM: CHEATING WITH WORDS.` · `PUBLIC SHAME IS LIKE BLOODSHED.` · `MONEY RETURNS. WORDS DON'T.` · then, large: `YE SHALL NOT WRONG ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one hurtful remark before it's said. Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two for a moment when a sharp line rose up in you: a reply to a text, a comment about someone's cooking, a joke at a sibling's expense. Replay it slowly. Notice the tiny gap between thinking the words and saying them. That gap is where today's verse lives. Rest there for a few breaths, so you'll recognize it next time it opens. The bell holds the time.
Ona'at devarim. Wronging with words: cheating someone of their dignity the way a bad merchant cheats them of money.
Your line: words can wrong. Today, before one reply, in person or on a screen, ask whether it would raise someone's face or drain it. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching treats hurtful speech as a serious wrong; the laws of ona'at devarim, from Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 and the Talmud's discussion at 58b, are studied alongside the laws of gossip, and public embarrassment is counted among the gravest harms.

fork.setup: you're browsing a shop with no plan to buy. you like a bowl. what does the Mishnah say about asking its price?
options: don't ask if you have no intention of buying.
ask, but only on a quiet day.
fork.reveal: Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 lists it as ona'at devarim: you raise the seller's hope with no plan to fulfill it.

original.note: Hebrew: wronging with words. ona'ah is overcharging; devarim, words.

trapdoor: what you thought: "don't wrong one another" is about fair prices.
what it means: the rabbis read the second time the Torah says it as a ban on hurtful words.
what a scholar hears: Bava Metzia 58b infers this from the doubled phrase in Leviticus 25:14 and 25:17; the rule is built on a repetition.

sources.quoted: And ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God; for I am the LORD your God.

notes: Leviticus 25:17 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; please confirm.

Examples from Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 (pricing without intent to buy; reminding a penitent of past deeds) and the Gemara at 58b (Job's friends; public shaming likened to bloodshed; the teaching that verbal wronging is greater than monetary, with reasons). Confirm: the Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai for 'greater', and the 'money can be returned' reason to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani.
The Mishnah's convert example was left out for brevity; a Keeper may prefer it included.
